prompt: Each lattice point of the plane is labeled by a positive integer. Each of these numbers is the arithmetic mean of its four neighbors (above, below, left, right). Show that all the numbers are equal.
answer: All numbers are equal (by showing the minimum equals the maximum via the mean condition).

solutions.title: The minimum spreads everywhere
solutions.body:
The labels are positive integers, so some label $m$ is the smallest. At a point labeled $m$, the four neighbors $a,b,c,d$ satisfy $m=\frac{a+b+c+d}{4}$ with each of $a,b,c,d\ge m$. Equality forces $a=b=c=d=m$.

So every neighbor of a point labeled $m$ is also labeled $m$. Since any lattice point can be reached from any other by steps between neighbors, every point is labeled $m$. ∎

prompt: Determine, with proof, whether $22!\,6!+1$ is prime.
answer: Not prime: $22!\,6!+1$ is divisible by 29 (by Wilson's theorem).

solutions.title: Wilson's theorem mod 29
solutions.body:
By Wilson's theorem, $28!\equiv-1\pmod{29}$. Now
$$28!=22!\cdot(23\cdot24\cdot25\cdot26\cdot27\cdot28)\equiv22!\cdot\big((-6)(-5)(-4)(-3)(-2)(-1)\big)=22!\cdot6!\pmod{29},$$
since there are six negative factors. Hence $22!\,6!\equiv-1\pmod{29}$, so $29\mid 22!\,6!+1$. As $22!\,6!+1>29$, it is not prime. ∎

prompt: Is there a number $s$ in the set $\{\pi,2\pi,3\pi,\ldots\}$ such that the first three digits after the decimal point of $s$ are .001? Fully justify your answer.
answer: Yes, such $s$ exists. By Weyl's equidistribution theorem (or the density of $\{n\pi \bmod 1\}$), multiples of $\pi$ are dense in $[0,1]$, so some $n\pi$ has fractional part in $(0.001, 0.002)$.

solutions.title: Pigeonhole on fractional parts
solutions.body:
Yes. Split $[0,1)$ into 1000 intervals of length $\frac1{1000}$. Among the fractional parts of $\pi,2\pi,\ldots,1001\pi$, two, say of $i\pi$ and $j\pi$ with $i<j$, fall in the same interval. Then $\{(j-i)\pi\}$ is within $\frac1{1000}$ of $0$ or of $1$, and it is not $0$ because $\pi$ is irrational. So for $d=j-i$, the fractional part $\varepsilon=\{d\pi\}$ satisfies $0<\varepsilon<\frac1{1000}$ or $1-\frac1{1000}<\varepsilon<1$.

In the first case the multiples $kd\pi$ ($k=1,2,\ldots$) have fractional parts increasing in steps of $\varepsilon<\frac1{1000}$ until they pass 1, so one of them lands in $[0.001,0.002)$. In the second case they decrease in steps of $1-\varepsilon<\frac1{1000}$, and the same argument applies. That multiple $s$ of $\pi$ has first three decimal digits $.001$. ∎

prompt:
For any nonnegative integer $r$, let $S_r$ be a function whose domain is the natural numbers that satisfies $$S_r(p^\alpha)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }p\le r;\\ p^{\alpha-1}(p-r),&\text{if }p>r\end{cases}$$ for all primes $p$ and positive integers $\alpha$, and that $S_r(ab)=S_r(a)S_r(b)$ whenever $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime.

Now, suppose there are $n$ squirrels at a party. Each squirrel is labeled with a unique number from the set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$. Two squirrels are friends with each other if and only if the difference between their labels is relatively prime to $n$. For example, if $n=10$, then the squirrels with labels 3 and 10 are friends with each other because $10-3=7$, and 7 is relatively prime to 10.

Fix a positive integer $m$. Define a *clique* of size $m$ to be any set of $m$ squirrels at the party with the property that any two squirrels in the clique are friends with each other. Determine, with proof, a formula (using $S_r$) for the number of cliques of size $m$ at the squirrel party.

solutions.title: Count ordered cliques prime by prime
solutions.body:
Two labels $i,j$ are friends iff no prime $p\mid n$ divides $i-j$, i.e. $i\not\equiv j\pmod p$ for every prime $p\mid n$. So a set of $m$ labels is a clique iff, for each prime $p\mid n$, its elements have $m$ distinct residues mod $p$.

Count ordered $m$-tuples $(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ of distinct labels forming a clique. Write $n=\prod p^{\alpha}$. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, choosing the tuple is the same as choosing, independently for each $p^\alpha\,\|\,n$, a tuple of residues mod $p^\alpha$ whose reductions mod $p$ are distinct. For one prime power: $x_1$ has $p^\alpha$ choices, $x_2$ has $p^{\alpha}-p^{\alpha-1}=p^{\alpha-1}(p-1)$ choices (avoid $x_1$'s class mod $p$), and in general $x_{r+1}$ has $p^{\alpha-1}(p-r)$ choices, or $0$ once $r\ge p$. That is exactly $S_r(p^\alpha)$, so the number for $p^\alpha$ is $\prod_{r=0}^{m-1}S_r(p^\alpha)$.

Multiplying over the prime powers and using multiplicativity, the number of ordered cliques is $\prod_{r=0}^{m-1}S_r(n)$. Each clique is counted $m!$ times, so the number of cliques of size $m$ is
$$\frac{S_0(n)S_1(n)\cdots S_{m-1}(n)}{m!}.$$
(Check: for $n$ prime this is $\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-m+1)}{m!}=\binom nm$, as every pair is friends.) ∎
